details.what: Acne is a common condition involving hair follicles and oil glands.
details.notice: Blackheads, whiteheads, inflamed bumps, or lingering marks.
details.why: Oil production, clogged follicles, inflammation, and hormonal changes may contribute.
details.similar: Rosacea, folliculitis, and other facial bumps.
details.treatment: Gentle skin care and clinician-selected topical, oral, or procedural options.
details.next: Note your routine and avoid picking; ask about suitable care for your skin.
details.when: If acne is painful, scarring, persistent, or affecting your wellbeing.

details.what: Eczema describes inflammatory skin conditions that often affect the skin barrier.
details.notice: Itch, dryness, patches of irritation, or changes in skin texture.
details.why: Skin-barrier differences and environmental triggers can play a role.
details.similar: Contact dermatitis, psoriasis, and fungal rashes.
details.treatment: Moisturizing, trigger review, and clinician-advised anti-inflammatory care.
details.next: Keep track of products and situations that seem to irritate your skin.
details.when: If symptoms persist, disrupt sleep, become painful, or show signs of infection.

details.what: Psoriasis is an inflammatory condition that can affect skin and sometimes nails or joints.
details.notice: Well-defined patches with scale; appearances vary across skin tones.
details.why: Immune activity and inherited factors may contribute.
details.similar: Eczema, seborrheic dermatitis, or fungal conditions.
details.treatment: A clinician may discuss topical care, light therapy, or other treatments.
details.next: Note affected areas and mention any joint discomfort at a consultation.
details.when: If patches spread, are uncomfortable, or joint symptoms occur.

details.what: Rosacea is a recurring inflammatory condition commonly affecting the central face.
details.notice: Flushing, persistent color changes, sensitivity, or bumps.
details.why: Multiple factors may be involved; individual triggers can vary.
details.similar: Acne, contact irritation, and other facial rashes.
details.treatment: Gentle care, trigger awareness, and clinician-selected treatments.
details.next: Note recurring triggers and mention any eye discomfort.
details.when: If facial changes persist or your eyes become irritated.

details.what: Contact dermatitis is skin inflammation after contact with an irritant or allergen.
details.notice: Itching, redness or color change, dryness, or a rash where contact occurred.
details.why: Products, metals, fragrances, or workplace exposures may be involved.
details.similar: Eczema, fungal rashes, and other inflammatory conditions.
details.treatment: Identifying exposures, gentle care, and clinician-advised treatment.
details.next: Make a list of recently used products and possible exposures.
details.when: If a reaction is severe, recurrent, widespread, or difficult to explain.

details.what: Seborrheic dermatitis is a recurring inflammatory condition often affecting oil-rich areas.
details.notice: Flakes, itch, or irritated areas on the scalp, face, or around the ears.
details.why: Skin inflammation and responses to naturally present scalp yeast may contribute.
details.similar: Dandruff, scalp psoriasis, eczema, or fungal infection.
details.treatment: Medicated cleansing and other treatments selected by a clinician.
details.next: Note which areas are affected and how often symptoms return.
details.when: If irritation persists, spreads, or does not improve with appropriate care.

details.what: Vitiligo involves loss of pigment in areas of skin.
details.notice: Light or white patches that can appear in different locations.
details.why: Immune-related processes may affect pigment-producing cells.
details.similar: Other causes of lighter patches, including post-inflammatory changes.
details.treatment: Sun protection and clinician-guided options depending on the individual.
details.next: Record when and where changes appeared for a consultation.
details.when: If new patches appear or existing patches change.

conditions.title: Melasma
conditions.keywords: dark spots pigmentation uneven skin tone

details.what: Melasma is a form of increased skin pigmentation, often on the face.
details.notice: Gradual patches of darker color, sometimes in a symmetric pattern.
details.why: Sun exposure and hormonal factors may contribute.
details.similar: Post-inflammatory pigmentation and other pigment changes.
details.treatment: Consistent sun protection and clinician-guided skin care or procedures.
details.next: Discuss your skin-care routine and sun exposure with a professional.
details.when: If pigmentation is new, changing, or concerning to you.

details.what: Pattern hair loss is a gradual change in hair density with characteristic patterns.
details.notice: A widening part, reduced volume, or gradual thinning at the hairline or crown.
details.why: Genetic and hormonal factors can contribute.
details.similar: Telogen effluvium, breakage, and other forms of hair loss.
details.treatment: A clinician may discuss established medical or procedural options.
details.next: Note the timeline and any family history before a consultation.
details.when: If thinning progresses or you are unsure what is causing it.

details.what: Telogen effluvium is a pattern of increased hair shedding.
details.notice: More hairs than usual shedding across the scalp.
details.why: Physical stress, illness, or other changes may precede shedding.
details.similar: Pattern hair loss and other causes of diffuse shedding.
details.treatment: Assessment of possible contributing factors and supportive hair care.
details.next: Note when shedding began and any major changes beforehand.
details.when: If shedding is rapid, prolonged, or accompanied by scalp symptoms.

details.what: Alopecia areata is an immune-related form of hair loss.
details.notice: One or more areas of reduced hair, sometimes appearing suddenly.
details.why: Immune activity affects hair follicles; the course varies between people.
details.similar: Fungal scalp infection, traction, or other patchy hair loss.
details.treatment: A dermatologist can discuss observation or suitable treatment options.
details.next: Arrange an assessment rather than assuming the cause of a patch.
details.when: For new or rapidly changing patches of hair loss.

details.what: Dandruff describes visible scalp flaking, often with mild irritation.
details.notice: Loose flakes and sometimes an itchy scalp.
details.why: Several scalp processes can contribute to flaking.
details.similar: Seborrheic dermatitis, scalp psoriasis, or irritation.
details.treatment: Appropriate scalp cleansing or clinician-recommended products.
details.next: Note the severity and whether irritation or redness is present.
details.when: If flaking is persistent, painful, or accompanied by hair loss.

details.what: Scalp psoriasis is psoriasis affecting the scalp.
details.notice: Thick scale, itch, and defined areas of inflammation.
details.similar: Dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis, or other scalp conditions.
details.treatment: Clinician-guided scalp treatments and follow-up when needed.
details.next: Avoid forcefully removing scales and discuss persistent symptoms.
details.when: If scalp symptoms are painful, persistent, or extensive.

conditions.title: Tinea Capitis
conditions.keywords: tinea capitis scalp fungal patchy hair loss

details.what: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp that needs professional assessment.
details.notice: Scaly areas, broken hairs, or areas of reduced hair; presentations vary.
details.why: Certain fungi can spread through close contact or shared items.
details.similar: Scalp psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, or alopecia areata.
details.treatment: A clinician determines whether testing and prescription treatment are needed.
details.next: Arrange an evaluation and avoid sharing combs or headwear until assessed.
details.when: Promptly for suspected infection, particularly with pain, pus, or hair loss.

details.what: Hair breakage happens when strands snap along their length rather than shed from the root.
details.notice: Short uneven strands, split ends, or reduced length retention.
details.why: Heat, chemical processing, tension, and other factors may weaken strands.
details.similar: Hair shedding or other forms of hair loss.
details.treatment: Gentler handling and addressing contributing practices or conditions.
details.next: Review styling habits and note whether hair is shedding or snapping.
details.when: If breakage is substantial, sudden, or occurs with scalp changes.
